topic: Vision, strategy, goals and the business model

notes.front: What is the business model canvas?
notes.back: A strategic management template: a visual chart describing a firm's or product's value proposition, infrastructure, customers and finances.
notes.explanation: Its point is to put the elements of a business, or of one product, on a single visual chart.
notes.evidence: It offers a visual chart with elements describing a firm's or product's
notes.example: Like a one-page floor plan of a business, but instead of rooms it has boxes for who is served, what they are offered, and how money comes in and goes out.

notes.front: On the business model canvas, what is a value proposition?
notes.back: The collection of products and services a business offers to meet its customers' needs.
notes.explanation: The block is described from the customer's side: it is what the business offers to meet their needs, whether products, services or both.
notes.evidence: The collection of products and services a business offers to meet the needs of its customers.
notes.example: Like the line on a bakery's window saying “fresh bread by 7 a.m., baked on site”, but written down as one box of the canvas.

notes.front: On the business model canvas, what are customer segments?
notes.back: The groups of customers a company tries to serve, divided by their different needs and attributes.
notes.explanation: The article says a company must identify which customers it tries to serve in order to build an effective business model.
notes.evidence: To build an effective business model, a company must identify which customers it tries to serve. Various sets of customers can be segmented based on their different needs and attributes
notes.example: Like a bus company that plans separately for daily commuters and for weekend tourists, because each group needs something different.

notes.front: According to the EBM Guide, what do goals lack without effective Mission and Vision statements?
notes.back: A compelling purpose, especially for people working under conditions of uncertainty.
notes.explanation: The Guide treats purpose and goals as two halves: goals make concrete progress, while Mission and Vision give that progress its reason.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Purpose of the EBM Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Organizations form goals to make concrete progress toward achieving their Mission and Vision. Without goals, the Mission and Vision are simply lofty aspirations. Furthermore, without effective Mission and Vision statements goals lack a compelling purpose, especially for those working under conditions of uncertainty.

notes.front: A city transport firm unveils an inspiring Vision Statement: “Nobody waits more than five minutes for a ride.” A year later no team can say what it is working toward, and the Product Owner is told to “just build toward the vision”. What does the EBM Guide say is missing?
notes.back: D: Goals, at several levels, that turn the vision into concrete progress
notes.choices:
A) A longer, more detailed Vision Statement
B) A new Mission Statement to replace the vision
C) A bigger Product Backlog of features
D) Goals, at several levels, that turn the vision into concrete progress
notes.choicesExplained: A: the vision is not the gap; without goals, the Guide calls Mission and Vision simply lofty aspirations. C: more features are outputs, not goals that show progress toward the vision. B: a Mission Statement says why the firm is uniquely capable; it does not add goals.
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide says organisations form goals to make concrete progress toward their Mission and Vision; without them the vision stays an aspiration.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Purpose of the EBM Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Organizations form goals to make concrete progress toward achieving their Mission and Vision. Without goals, the Mission and Vision are simply lofty aspirations.

notes.front: A Scrum Team is handed a quarterly target list by management, with no word on why the organisation exists or what change it wants to make. The work is highly uncertain, and the Developers ask the Product Owner why any of it matters. What does the EBM Guide suggest is lacking?
notes.back: D: Effective Mission and Vision statements that give the goals a compelling purpose
notes.choices:
A) More detailed acceptance criteria on each target
B) A stricter Definition of Done
C) Nothing: under uncertainty, targets alone are enough
D) Effective Mission and Vision statements that give the goals a compelling purpose
notes.choicesExplained: A: detail on the work does not supply a purpose; the Guide ties purpose to Mission and Vision. B: the Definition of Done is about Increment quality, not about why the goals matter. C: the Guide says the opposite: under uncertainty, goals without Mission and Vision lack a compelling purpose.
notes.explanation: The Guide stresses purpose most for people working under conditions of uncertainty, which is this team's situation.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Purpose of the EBM Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: without effective Mission and Vision statements goals lack a compelling purpose, especially for those working under conditions of uncertainty.

notes.front: In the EBM Guide, what does achieving a Strategic Goal result in for the people it targets?
notes.back: Improved happiness, safety, security or well-being for the recipients of a product or service.
notes.explanation: The Guide links this to Unrealized Value: the goal closes a satisfaction gap between what beneficiaries want and what they experience now.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Setting Goals”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Achieving the goal results in improved happiness, safety, security, or well-being of the recipients of some product or service. In EBM, we refer to this as Unrealized Value, which is the satisfaction gap between a beneficiary’s desired outcome and their current experience.

notes.front: A Product Owner for a pharmacy app drafts four candidate Strategic Goals. Which best fits the EBM Guide's description of a Strategic Goal?
notes.back: A: Patients with long-term conditions never run out of the medicine they need
notes.choices:
A) Patients with long-term conditions never run out of the medicine they need
B) Move the app to a new cloud platform by the third quarter
C) Ship forty new features this year
D) Grow the company's revenue by a fifth
notes.choicesExplained: B: this is an activity or means, not an outcome for a group of people. C: features are outputs; they do not by themselves show a better outcome for anyone. D: revenue is an impact for the organisation, not an unrealised outcome for a specific group.
notes.explanation: The Guide says a Strategic Goal usually aims at a highly desirable but unrealised outcome for a specific group of people.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Setting Goals”, p. 5
notes.evidence: The Strategic Goal is usually focused on achieving a highly desirable but unrealized outcome for a specific group of people.

notes.front: A director proposes the Strategic Goal “Become number one in market share for home insurance.” How should a Product Owner guided by EBM respond?
notes.back: C: Reframe it around a desirable outcome that a specific group of people does not yet have
notes.choices:
A) Accept it: market share is the clearest Strategic Goal
B) Turn it into a list of features that competitors already have
C) Reframe it around a desirable outcome that a specific group of people does not yet have
D) Drop goals and let the Product Backlog order speak for itself
notes.choicesExplained: A: market share is an impact; the Guide says Strategic Goals usually target an unrealised outcome for people. B: a feature list is output, and it names means rather than a desired outcome. D: the Guide says organisations must define measurable goals; dropping them removes the target.
notes.explanation: Achieving a Strategic Goal, in the Guide's words, improves the happiness, safety, security or well-being of the recipients of a product, which market share alone does not describe.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Setting Goals”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Achieving the goal results in improved happiness, safety, security, or well-being of the recipients of some product or service.

notes.front: Besides whether progress is being made, what does measuring a Strategic Goal help you understand?
notes.back: Whether the Strategic Goal is still relevant across time.
notes.explanation: The Guide gives measurement two jobs here: tracking progress and checking that the goal still matters.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Setting Goals”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Measurement is important to understand if progress is being made and if the strategic goal is relevant across time.

notes.front: In the EBM Guide, why should measurable goals, measures and experiments be made transparent?
notes.back: To encourage organisational alignment.
notes.explanation: The Guide pairs this with a rule that goals must be measurable, so that everyone can see whether each goal is achieved.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Setting Goals”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Organizations must define measurable goals that will indicate whether that goal is achieved. These measurable goals, measures, and experiments should be made transparent in order to encourage organizational alignment.

notes.front: A Product Owner's Strategic Goal is “Commuters get to work without stress.” The board asks whether things are improving, and nobody can say. What should the Product Owner do first?
notes.back: C: Define a measure for the goal, so progress and the goal's continued relevance can be seen
notes.choices:
A) Report the number of features released as the measure of progress
B) Leave it unmeasured, because Strategic Goals are meant to be aspirational
C) Define a measure for the goal, so progress and the goal's continued relevance can be seen
D) Replace it with an activity, such as “add 50 buses”, which is easy to count
notes.choicesExplained: A: features released are outputs and do not show whether commuters' experience improved. B: the Guide says organisations must define measurable goals. D: the Guide warns that an activity needed to reach a goal is not the goal itself.
notes.explanation: The Guide says measurement shows both whether progress is being made and whether the Strategic Goal is still relevant.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Setting Goals”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Measurement is important to understand if progress is being made and if the strategic goal is relevant across time.

notes.front: Two years into a Strategic Goal to cut the time small firms spend on tax forms, a new law removes most of the forms. The measures show the gap has almost closed on its own. What should the Product Owner do?
notes.back: C: Inspect whether the Strategic Goal is still relevant and adapt it if needed
notes.choices:
A) Stop measuring, since the goal is nearly met
B) Keep the goal unchanged until its original deadline
C) Inspect whether the Strategic Goal is still relevant and adapt it if needed
D) Ask the Developers to work faster on the remaining forms
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide expects goals to change because of outside events; holding on ignores the evidence. A: measures are what revealed the change; the Guide uses them to judge relevance. D: speed does not answer whether the goal still matters.
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide says goals can change because of outside events and asks whether Intermediate and Strategic Goals are still relevant or need adapting.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Goals can change because of outside events, and your tactics to reach your goals may need to be reconsidered and revised, for example: ○ Was the Immediate Tactical Goal the right goal? ○ Are the Intermediate and Strategic Goals still relevant or do they need to be adapted?

notes.front: A bike-share scheme writes: “This Sprint, test whether showing live dock availability in the app reduces failed trips.” Which EBM goal level does this most likely describe?
notes.back: A: Immediate Tactical Goal
notes.choices:
A) Immediate Tactical Goal
B) Intermediate Goal
C) Product Goal
D) Strategic Goal
notes.choicesExplained: D: it is a near-term test, not the far, uncertain outcome. B: it is not an achievement that shows the scheme is on the path; it is the current focus. C: it is a short experiment for one Sprint, not the Scrum Team's long-term objective.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes Immediate Tactical Goals as critical near-term objectives toward which a team or group of teams will work.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Setting Goals”, p. 5
notes.evidence: These are critical near-term objectives toward which a team or group of teams will work.

notes.front: In the EBM Guide, what does considering both Current Value and Unrealized Value give an organisation?
notes.back: A way to balance present and possible future benefits.
notes.explanation: The Guide presents the two Key Value Areas as a pair: one for present benefits, one for possible future ones.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: The consideration of both CV and UV provides organizations with a way to balance present and possible future benefits.

notes.front: Survey data for a tax-filing app shows salaried users are satisfied, but self-employed users cannot file with it at all and want to. The Product Owner is framing a new Strategic Goal. Which starting point does the EBM Guide support?
notes.back: B: The self-employed users' satisfaction gap, as a chance to reduce Unrealized Value by raising Current Value
notes.choices:
A) The feature list of the leading competitor
B) The self-employed users' satisfaction gap, as a chance to reduce Unrealized Value by raising Current Value
C) The Developers' average output per Sprint
D) Next year's revenue target
notes.choicesExplained: A: copying features says nothing about a satisfaction gap for a specific group. C: delivery capability matters for planning, but the Guide forms Strategic Goals from a satisfaction gap. D: revenue is an impact; the Guide forms Strategic Goals from a gap and an opportunity to decrease UV.
notes.explanation: The Guide says Strategic Goals are formed from some satisfaction gap and an opportunity to decrease UV by increasing CV.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Strategic Goals are formed from some satisfaction gap and an opportunity for an organization to decrease UV by increasing CV.

notes.front: Research on a mature invoicing product shows customers are very satisfied, the market is saturated and nobody reports an unmet need. A manager still wants a bold new Strategic Goal for it. What question does EBM point the Product Owner to?
notes.back: A: Whether further investment to capture Unrealized Value is worth the effort and risk
notes.choices:
A) Whether further investment to capture Unrealized Value is worth the effort and risk
B) How to raise output per Sprint
C) Which features to add so the Product Backlog stays full
D) How to keep the Strategic Goal secret from customers
notes.choicesExplained: C: a full backlog is not a reason to invest; EBM asks whether untapped value exists. B: output does not answer whether any unrealised value is left to capture. D: EBM asks for transparent goals, and secrecy does not address the missing gap.
notes.explanation: Strategic Goals come from a satisfaction gap; with no gap, the Guide's Unrealized Value questions ask whether more effort and investment are warranted.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Unrealized Value (UV)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: 2. Is it worth the effort and risk to pursue these untapped opportunities? 3. Should further investments be made to capture additional Unrealized Value?

notes.front: A company creates one Scrum Team for “everything the technology department does”. Nobody can say where this product starts or ends, and its users are “anyone, really”. What does the Scrum Guide's description of a product show is missing?
notes.back: A: A clear boundary and well-defined users or customers
notes.choices:
A) A clear boundary and well-defined users or customers
B) A physical form: only physical things count as products
C) A written Product Vision signed by executives
D) More Developers, so every technology task can be covered
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide says a product could be a service, a physical product or something more abstract. C: the Guide's attributes are a boundary, stakeholders and users, not a signed vision. D: team size does not create a boundary or define users.
notes.explanation: The Guide says a product has a clear boundary, known stakeholders and well-defined users or customers; this one lacks the first and third.
notes.evidence: A product is a vehicle to deliver value. It has a clear boundary, known stakeholders, well-defined users or customers.

notes.front: An internal payroll service is used by staff only and is never sold. A manager says it cannot have a Product Owner because it is “not a real product”. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: B: It can be a product: a product could be a service, with a clear boundary, known stakeholders and defined users
notes.choices:
A) It is not a product, because a product must be sold to paying customers
B) It can be a product: a product could be a service, with a clear boundary, known stakeholders and defined users
C) It becomes a product only once it has a Nexus of several teams
D) It is a product only if it is physical
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide defines a product by boundary, stakeholders and users, not by sales. D: the Guide says a product could be a service, a physical product or something more abstract. C: the number of teams does not decide whether something is a product.
notes.explanation: The Guide's definition is broad: a product could be a service, a physical product, or something more abstract.
notes.evidence: It has a clear boundary, known stakeholders, well-defined users or customers. A product could be a service, a physical product, or something more abstract.

notes.front: The Product Goal is “Small shops can take card payments without a terminal.” This Sprint the team delivered a polished internal admin report that meets the Definition of Done but has nothing to do with payments. How should the Product Owner see it?
notes.back: A: It is Done work, but it is not a stepping stone toward the Product Goal; refocus the ordering on the goal
notes.choices:
A) It is Done work, but it is not a stepping stone toward the Product Goal; refocus the ordering on the goal
B) It is not an Increment at all, because it is unrelated to the goal
C) It is fine: any Done work moves the Product Goal forward
D) Cancel the Sprint, because the Sprint Goal was wrong
notes.choicesExplained: B: work that meets the Definition of Done is part of an Increment; the issue is focus, not status. C: the Guide calls an Increment a stepping stone toward the Product Goal, and this one does not step toward it. D: cancellation is for a Sprint Goal that becomes obsolete, and this Sprint is already over.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls each Increment a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal, and this one does not lead there.
notes.evidence: An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified

notes.front: For the Product Goal “Small shops can take card payments without a terminal”, which planned Sprint outcome is the best stepping stone?
notes.back: D: A usable tap-to-pay flow for one common card type, meeting the Definition of Done
notes.choices:
A) A design document covering every card type
B) Half-built support for all card types, none of it usable yet
C) A marketing plan for the launch
D) A usable tap-to-pay flow for one common card type, meeting the Definition of Done
notes.choicesExplained: A: a document is not a usable Increment. B: the Guide says the Increment must be usable to provide value. C: a plan is not an Increment of the product.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls the Increment a concrete stepping stone and says it must be usable to provide value.
notes.evidence: An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified, ensuring that all Increments work together. In order to provide value, the Increment must be usable.

notes.front: At the Sprint Review, the Scrum Team presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and {{c1::progress toward the Product Goal}} is discussed.
notes.explanation: Presenting results and discussing the Product Goal happen together, with key stakeholders present.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed.

notes.front: At every Sprint Review the Product Owner shows new screens, and stakeholders leave asking, “But are we any closer to the Product Goal?” What should change?
notes.back: D: Discuss progress toward the Product Goal with the stakeholders at the Sprint Review
notes.choices:
A) Hold a separate monthly steering meeting for Product Goal progress
B) Cover it at the Sprint Retrospective
C) Report Product Goal progress at the Daily Scrum
D) Discuss progress toward the Product Goal with the stakeholders at the Sprint Review
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide places this discussion in the Sprint Review; extra meetings are what Scrum's events aim to replace. C: the Daily Scrum is for the Developers and inspects progress toward the Sprint Goal. B: the Retrospective plans ways to increase quality and effectiveness, with the Scrum Team only.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the Scrum Team presents results to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed at the Sprint Review.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed.

notes.front: This Sprint the team mostly strengthened the product's infrastructure, so there are few new screens to show. A stakeholder suggests skipping the Sprint Review. What should the Product Owner propose?
notes.back: A: Hold it: inspect the outcome and discuss progress toward the Product Goal, then decide next steps together
notes.choices:
A) Hold it: inspect the outcome and discuss progress toward the Product Goal, then decide next steps together
B) Skip it this time and send a written summary instead
C) Hold it, but only with the Scrum Team
D) Postpone it until there are enough new features
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide describes the Sprint Review as a working session, not a report that can be mailed. C: the Guide says results are presented to key stakeholders. D: the Sprint Review is part of every Sprint, whatever the Sprint produced.
notes.explanation: The Sprint Review's purpose is to inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations, including progress toward the Product Goal.
notes.evidence: The purpose of the Sprint Review is to inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations. The Scrum Team presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed.

notes.front: A Product Goal was to help clinics file a paper form online. A new regulation abolishes the form. What may the Product Owner do?
notes.back: C: Abandon the Product Goal and develop the next one
notes.choices:
A) Keep the goal until it is fulfilled, since goals may not be dropped
B) Wait for the stakeholders to vote on a new goal
C) Abandon the Product Goal and develop the next one
D) Keep working on it and review it next year
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide allows a goal to be fulfilled or abandoned. B: the Product Owner is not a committee and is accountable for the Product Goal. D: the evidence already shows the goal no longer has value.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the team must fulfil or abandon one objective before taking on the next, so abandoning is a legitimate choice.
notes.evidence: The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team. They must fulfill (or abandon) one objective before taking on the next.

notes.front: The measures show the Product Goal has been fulfilled. What is the Product Owner accountable for next?
notes.back: C: Developing and explicitly communicating the next Product Goal
notes.choices:
A) Disbanding the Scrum Team, since the product is finished
B) Letting the Developers choose the next Product Goal
C) Developing and explicitly communicating the next Product Goal
D) Waiting for the annual planning cycle
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Product Goal is one objective; the Product Owner develops the next one. B: developing the Product Goal is part of the Product Owner's accountability. D: the Guide puts no such wait on the next objective.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal as part of the Product Owner's Product Backlog management.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner is also accountable for effective Product Backlog management, which includes: - Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal;

notes.front: Osterwalder's business model canvas has {{c1::nine}} boxes, or building blocks.
notes.explanation: The article lists them as customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships and cost structure.
notes.evidence: Osterwalder's canvas has nine boxes: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships, and cost structure.

notes.front: Which business model canvas block covers how a company gets its value proposition to its targeted customers?
notes.back: Channels.
notes.explanation: The article says effective channels distribute the value proposition in ways that are fast, efficient and cost-effective.
notes.evidence: A company can deliver its value proposition to its targeted customers through different channels. Effective channels will distribute a company's value proposition in ways that are fast, efficient and cost-effective.

notes.front: Which business model canvas block addresses how the business will win new customers, keep them and grow revenue from them?
notes.back: Customer relationships.
notes.explanation: The article names these as three critical steps of a customer's relationship that the block should address.
notes.evidence: That element should address three critical steps of a customer's relationship: How the business will get new customers, how the business will keep customers purchasing or using its services and how the business will grow its revenue from its current customers.

notes.front: Which business model canvas block describes the way a company makes income from each customer segment?
notes.back: Revenue streams.
notes.explanation: The block is tied to customer segments: income is looked at for each segment the company serves.
notes.evidence: Revenue streams: The way a company makes income from each customer segment.

notes.front: Which business model canvas block holds what is needed to create value for the customer, whether human, financial, physical or intellectual?
notes.back: Key resources.
notes.explanation: The article describes these as assets the company needs to sustain and support the business.
notes.evidence: The resources that are necessary to create value for the customer. They are considered assets to a company that are needed to sustain and support the business.

notes.front: Which business model canvas block lists the most important activities in executing a company's value proposition?
notes.back: Key activities.
notes.explanation: The article's example is a pen maker building an efficient supply chain to drive down costs.
notes.evidence: Key activities: The most important activities in executing a company's value proposition. An example for Bic, the pen manufacturer, would be creating an efficient supply chain to drive down costs.

notes.front: Which business model canvas block covers the buyer-supplier relationships and alliances a company cultivates so it can focus on its core activity?
notes.back: Key partnerships (described in the article as the partner network).
notes.explanation: The article says organisations cultivate these relationships to optimise operations and reduce the risks of a business model.
notes.evidence: In order to optimize operations and reduce risks of a business model, organizations usually cultivate buyer-supplier relationships so they can focus on their core activity.

notes.front: Which business model canvas block describes the most important monetary consequences of operating under a business model?
notes.back: Cost structure.
notes.explanation: It is the canvas's view of what running the chosen business model costs.
notes.evidence: This describes the most important monetary consequences while operating under different business models.

notes.front: A Product Owner at a meal-kit firm writes on the business model canvas: “Recipes that take five minutes, for busy parents, where rival kits take forty.” Which block is this?
notes.back: C: Value propositions
notes.choices:
A) Channels
B) Key activities
C) Value propositions
D) Revenue streams
notes.choicesExplained: A: channels are how the offer reaches customers, not what the offer is. B: key activities are what the company must do to execute the offer. D: revenue streams are how the company earns income from each segment.
notes.explanation: The article says a company's value proposition is what distinguishes it from its competitors, and this note does exactly that.
notes.evidence: a company's value proposition is what distinguishes it from its competitors.

notes.front: A Product Owner's delivery app serves hungry diners and, at the same time, the restaurants that cook for them; neither side would use it without the other. Which type of customer segments does the business model canvas article call this?
notes.back: B: Multi-sided platform or market
notes.choices:
A) Mass market
B) Multi-sided platform or market
C) Niche market
D) Diversify
notes.choicesExplained: A: a mass market has no specific segmentation; here two distinct groups depend on each other. C: a niche market segments customers by specialised needs and characteristics. D: a diversified business serves several segments with different needs, but the article does not describe them as depending on each other.
notes.explanation: The article describes some companies as serving mutually dependent customer segments, which is the case here.
notes.evidence: For a smooth day-to-day business operation, some companies will serve mutually dependent customer segments.

notes.front: Why has the business model canvas been characterised as static?
notes.back: It does not capture changes in strategy or the evolution of the model.
notes.explanation: The criticism is that strategy and the model evolve, and the canvas does not record that change.
notes.evidence: The business model canvas has been characterized as static because it does not capture changes in strategy or the evolution of the model

notes.front: What limit do critics link to the business model canvas's focus on organisations?
notes.back: Conceptual isolation from its environment, for example from the industry structure.
notes.explanation: The article presents this isolation as a consequence of the canvas's focus on organisations.
notes.evidence: Some limits of the template are its focus on organizations and its consequent conceptual isolation from its environment, whether this is related to the industry structure
